after: ## Issues at global, national and local level
alt: In October 2020 India and South Africa proposed waiving some IP rules for COVID-19 products at the WTO; in June 2022 a narrower decision let eligible members authorise vaccine production without the patent holder’s consent for five years. Supporters said patents slowed supply; many firms and some rich governments said patents fund research and that factories, materials and skills were the real limit.
caption: An issue that divides opinion: explain why each side holds its view.

after: ## Issues at global, national and local level
alt: Rings for the fictional town of Arnholt: locally, residents argue about a battery factory’s water use; nationally, the government offers a grant; globally, electric vehicle growth drives demand. A young resident supports it for jobs; a farmer opposes it over river water. The proposed action is approval with a binding water limit in dry months, enforced by independent monitoring.
caption: Local action can shape how a factory operates, not whether such factories are built.

after: ## Perspectives: who thinks what, and why
alt: The US CHIPS and Science Act, signed on 9 August 2022, provides $52.7 billion for semiconductor research, manufacturing and training. Supporters predict jobs and less reliance on imported chips, valuing security; critics say it gives taxpayers’ money to profitable firms, valuing fairness and competition. Both sides rest on predictions and values.
caption: When values differ, more data may not end the argument.

alt: Two causes, few technically trained workers and weak roads, power or internet, lead to consequences at three levels: young people leave, the country imports goods and earns less tax, and industry clusters in a few places. Below, an intended consequence of a factory (jobs) and a possible unintended one (higher house prices).
caption: Separate intended from unintended consequences, and present the latter as possible.

alt: Rwanda launched national drone delivery with Zipline on 14 October 2016, backed by Gavi and the UPS Foundation, first flying blood to remote clinics. Evaluation questions: early results came from parties with a vested interest; independent before-and-after comparisons would be stronger; and the model may not transfer to other countries.
caption: Innovation success stories need independent evidence and a transfer test.

alt: Bars show 75% of 60 start-ups funded by the fictional region of Talen (45 firms) still trading after three years, against 50% nationally. The weakness: the panel picked the most promising firms, which might have survived anyway, and the study’s author is not given. A fairer test compares funded firms with similar applicants who just missed out.
caption: A comparison is only fair if the groups were alike to begin with.

after: ## Courses of action and their effects
alt: A table of six actions with a benefit and drawback each: voluntary patent licensing, subsidies for new industry, conditions on new factories, right-to-repair rules, public research funding and training schemes with local colleges. The EU right-to-repair directive, adopted 13 June 2024 and due by 31 July 2026, is too new to judge its effects.
caption: Judge each action on cause, feasibility, winners and losers, sustainability and evidence.
